reception.text: An Associated Press dispatch reported that Roosevelt had before him reports of many instances of gross fraud and error under the naturalization laws, evils he had seen himself in New York City's government.
A second AP dispatch announced the three commissioners and said the work would "commence at once."

political_impact.text: The department heads chose the commissioners: Milton D. Purdy of Justice as chairman, Gaillard Hunt of State, and Richard K. Campbell of Commerce and Labor.
political_impact.source: Report of the Commission on Naturalization, H. Doc. 46, 59th Cong., 1st Sess.

political_impact.text: The commission counted 5,160 courts naturalizing aliens, 157 federal and 5,003 state, and recommended a uniform, federally supervised process.
political_impact.source: Report of the Commission on Naturalization, H. Doc. 46, p. 22

political_impact.text: The commission submitted its report on November 8, 1905, a week before its deadline.
political_impact.source: Report of the Commission on Naturalization, H. Doc. 46, letter of transmittal

political_impact.text: Roosevelt sent the commission's report to Congress.

legacy.text: The commission's report led directly to the Naturalization Act of 1906, which made the federal government the arbiter of naturalization and standardized the process and certificate nationwide.
The 1906 act renamed the Bureau of Immigration the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization, the institutional ancestor of today's citizenship service.
Commissioner Richard K. Campbell went on to head the bureau's Naturalization Division and served as Commissioner of Naturalization from 1913 to 1922.

later_actions.text: Congress passed the Naturalization Act, standardizing naturalization under federal supervision.

uncertain: The text of EO 296 has not been found in print; the signed original in the National Archives would settle its wording.

reception.text: The Audubon association printed the full order, with its lot acreages, in its annual report.

legacy.text: Stump Lake was the third federal bird reservation in the country and the first in North Dakota.
legacy.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Stump Lake NWR

legacy.text: Stump Lake and Devils Lake began rising in 1993; by 2005 the refuge islands were completely submerged, and they remain under 15 feet of water.
legacy.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Stump Lake NWR

today.name: Stump Lake National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: Administered from the Devils Lake Wetland Management District; closed to the public, its islands entirely under water.

related.note: Pelican Island, the first federal bird reservation (1903).
Breton Island, the second federal bird reservation (October 4, 1904).
The second Breton order, later in 1905, which can make Stump Lake look like the second reservation in the numbered series.
